```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(ermeeth2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

This page describes what a simulation returns and shows the usual ways of
handling it. Every example runs on a small database shipped with the package,
so the page reproduces without running a model.

## Getting the results

### From a simulation

`run_simulations()` returns the results and stores them in `data/output`,
under the `project_name` of the input configuration.

```{r}
#| eval: false
config <- readconfig(input_config_file  = file.path("configuration", "config_input_threeme.R"),
                     output_config_file = file.path("configuration", "config_output_threeme.R"))

data_full <- run_simulations(configuration = config)
```

### From a simulation already run

`read_3me_output()` reads a database back from `data/output`. The results are
stored as a parquet file by default, which lets the function read only what is
asked for: on a full model this is the difference between a few seconds and a
few minutes.

```{r}
#| eval: false
## everything
data_full <- read_3me_output("my_project")

## only what is needed: much faster on a large model
macro <- read_3me_output("my_project",
                         variables = c("GDP", "CH", "I", "X", "M"),
                         scenarios = c("baseline", "ct1"),
                         years     = 2020:2050)
```

When the input configuration sets `output_saved`, the results are also stored
with their sectors and commodities aggregated as the bridge of the
classification says. Those versions are read with `suffix`:

| `suffix` | Database |
|---|---|
| `NULL` (default) | the classification of the simulation |
| `"sec"` | sectors aggregated |
| `"com"` | commodities aggregated |
| `"sec_com"` | sectors and commodities aggregated |

```{r}
#| eval: false
data_agg <- read_3me_output("my_project", suffix = "sec_com")
```

### The database of this page

```{r}
#| label: load
data_full <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "minimodel.rds", package = "ermeeth2"))
```

It comes from a small training model: five variables, a baseline and one
scenario, `g`, an increase in government spending.

## What `data_full` looks like

`data_full` is a plain `data.frame` in **long format**: one line per
variable, year and scenario.

```{r}
#| label: head
head(data_full)
```

| Column | Type | Content |
|---|---|---|
| `variable` | character | Code of the variable, in upper case. |
| `year` | numeric | Period of the observation. |
| `scenario` | character | Name of the scenario, as in the input configuration. |
| `values` | numeric | Value in the scenario. |
| `values_ref` | numeric | Value in the baseline, for the same variable and year. |
| `index_scen` | numeric | 1 on the lines of the baseline, 0 on the others. |
| `sector` | character | Sector of the variable, `NA` if it has none. |
| `commodity` | character | Commodity of the variable, `NA` if it has none. |

A line is identified by `variable`, `year` and `scenario`. On the lines of the
baseline, `values` and `values_ref` are equal.

Because `values_ref` sits next to `values` on every line, comparing a scenario
with the baseline never needs a join.

### What is in it

```{r}
#| label: contents
unique(data_full$scenario)
unique(data_full$variable)
range(data_full$year)
```

On a full model there are thousands of variables. `variables_like()` finds
those whose code matches a regular expression:

```{r}
#| label: variables-like
variables_like(data_full, "^C", view = FALSE)
```

The dictionary says what a code means:

```{r}
#| label: dict
dict_labels(unique(data_full$variable))
dict_labels(unique(data_full$variable), lang = "fr")
```

## Selecting

Everything here is `dplyr::filter()`.

### One scenario

```{r}
#| label: one-scenario
shock <- data_full |> filter(scenario == "g")
head(shock, 3)
```

`index_scen` is a shortcut to leave the baseline out, whatever the scenarios
are called:

```{r}
#| label: no-baseline
data_full |> filter(index_scen == 0) |> distinct(scenario)
```

### A set of variables

```{r}
#| label: some-variables
activity <- data_full |> filter(variable %in% c("Y", "CH", "I"))
distinct(activity, variable)
```

### A period

```{r}
#| label: period
data_full |>
  filter(variable == "Y", scenario == "g", year %in% 2020:2024)
```

### A sector or a commodity

On a ThreeME database a sectoral variable has one code per sector, and the
`sector` column holds the name of the sector. Both can be used:

```{r}
#| eval: false
## the output of every sector
data_full |> filter(grepl("^Y_S", variable))

## everything about one sector
data_full |> filter(sector == "Construction")
```

## Computing

### Deviation from the baseline

By hand, since the baseline is on the same line:

```{r}
#| label: by-hand
data_full |>
  filter(scenario == "g", variable == "Y", year %in% 2020:2024) |>
  mutate(rel_diff = values / values_ref - 1,
         abs_diff = values - values_ref)
```

`threeme_transform()` does the same and knows the usual transformations. It
adds a `value` column, with the `transformation` used and its `unit`:

```{r}
#| label: transform
data_full |>
  filter(variable == "Y", year %in% 2020:2024) |>
  threeme_transform("reldiff") |>
  select(variable, year, scenario, values, values_ref, value, unit)
```

```{r}
#| label: transformations
#| echo: false
tr <- threeme_transformations()
data.frame(
  id = names(tr),
  meaning = vapply(tr, function(x) x$label, character(1)),
  row.names = NULL
)
```

One call can mix them, with a vector named by variable. The element without a
name is used for the variables that are not named:

```{r}
#| label: mixed
data_full |>
  filter(variable %in% c("Y", "MU"), year == 2025) |>
  threeme_transform(c(MU = "ppdiff", "reldiff")) |>
  select(variable, scenario, value, unit)
```

### Growth rates

```{r}
#| label: growth
data_full |>
  filter(variable == "Y", year %in% 2019:2023) |>
  threeme_transform("gr") |>
  select(variable, year, scenario, value)
```

By hand, the series has to be grouped and sorted first:

```{r}
#| label: growth-by-hand
data_full |>
  filter(variable == "Y") |>
  group_by(variable, scenario) |>
  arrange(year, .by_group = TRUE) |>
  mutate(growth = values / lag(values) - 1) |>
  ungroup() |>
  filter(year %in% 2020:2022)
```

### A new variable from existing ones

A ratio, a sum or a share needs the variables side by side. The steps are
always the same: keep the variables, put them in columns, compute, and put the
result back in lines so that it stacks under `data_full`.

`values` and `values_ref` are both carried along, so the new variable has its
own baseline and works with everything on this page.

```{r}
#| label: composite
share <- data_full |>
  filter(variable %in% c("CH", "Y")) |>
  select(variable, year, scenario, index_scen, values, values_ref) |>
  ## one column per variable, for the scenario and for the baseline
  pivot_wider(names_from = variable, values_from = c(values, values_ref)) |>
  ## the share of consumption in output
  mutate(values     = values_CH / values_Y,
         values_ref = values_ref_CH / values_ref_Y,
         variable   = "CH_SHARE") |>
  select(variable, year, scenario, index_scen, values, values_ref)

data_plus <- bind_rows(data_full, share)

data_plus |> filter(variable == "CH_SHARE", year == 2025)
```

The new variable is a share: its deviation is read in points. `value` is in
the unit of the variable, so -0.0077 on a share is -0.77 point.

```{r}
#| label: composite-use
data_plus |>
  filter(variable == "CH_SHARE", year %in% c(2021, 2025, 2030)) |>
  threeme_transform("ppdiff") |>
  select(variable, year, scenario, value, unit)
```

### A sum over sectors or commodities

On a ThreeME database, the lines of the sectors are summed after a `group_by()`
that leaves the sector out:

```{r}
#| eval: false
data_full |>
  filter(grepl("^EMS_S", variable)) |>
  group_by(year, scenario, index_scen) |>
  summarise(values = sum(values), values_ref = sum(values_ref), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(variable = "EMS_SECTORS")
```

A sum is only right for quantities. Prices and rates need a weighted mean:
this is what the aggregation rules of the package hold, and what the `sec`,
`com` and `sec_com` databases apply.

## From long to wide, and back

A table with one column per variable is easier to read, to export, and to
compute on.

```{r}
#| label: wide
wide <- data_full |>
  filter(scenario == "g") |>
  select(year, variable, values) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = variable, values_from = values)

head(wide, 4)
```

One column per scenario, to compare them:

```{r}
#| label: wide-scenarios
data_full |>
  filter(variable == "Y", year %in% 2020:2023) |>
  select(year, scenario, values) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = scenario, values_from = values)
```

And back to one line per variable:

```{r}
#| label: long
wide |>
  pivot_longer(-year, names_to = "variable", values_to = "values") |>
  head(4)
```

## Showing

### A plot

`simple_plot()` takes `data_full` as it is. The labels come from the
dictionary.

```{r}
#| label: fig-simple
#| fig-cap: "Deviation from the baseline"
simple_plot(data_full, c("Y", "CH", "I"))
```

The long format is also what `ggplot2` expects, for a plot of your own:

```{r}
#| label: fig-ggplot
#| fig-cap: "The same data, with ggplot2"
data_full |>
  filter(variable %in% c("Y", "CH", "I"), scenario == "g") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = values / values_ref - 1, colour = variable)) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, colour = NULL)
```

### A table

```{r}
#| label: tbl-simple
table_3me(data_full,
          variables = list(Activity = c("Y", "CH", "I"), Margins = "MU"),
          transformation = c(MU = "ppdiff", "reldiff"))
```

See [Graphs and tables with ermeeth2](graphs_and_tables.html) for what these
two functions can do.

## Saving

```{r}
#| eval: false
## as the simulations do: data/output/my_project.parquet
save_3me_output(data_plus, "my_project")

## a spreadsheet, one column per variable
data_full |>
  filter(scenario == "g") |>
  select(year, variable, values) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = variable, values_from = values) |>
  write.csv("results_g.csv", row.names = FALSE)
```
